lessons.osha-overview:
**What OSHA Is and Why It Exists — 29 CFR Part 1910**

OSHA — the Occupational Safety and Health Administration — was created under the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 (OSH Act). Congress passed the Act in response to rising rates of workplace injuries, illnesses, and fatalities. Before OSHA, there was no uniform federal system to ensure employers maintained safe conditions. The OSH Act gave the federal government the authority to set standards and enforce them.

OSHA's mission is to help ensure safe and healthful working conditions by setting and enforcing standards, and by providing training, outreach, education, and compliance assistance. OSHA is not solely an enforcement agency — it also partners with employers and workers through consultation programs, voluntary protection programs, and educational initiatives.

OSHA covers most private sector employers and their employees, as well as some public sector employers. OSHA's standards apply to many industries, including general industry (manufacturing, warehousing, services, healthcare, and maintenance), construction, maritime, and agriculture. Understanding what OSHA is and why it exists helps every worker recognize their own role in supporting a safer and healthier workplace.
lessons.general-industry-standards:
**General Industry Standards and Workplace Hazards — 29 CFR Part 1910**

OSHA's general industry standards are found in Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), Part 1910. Part 1910 contains standards that address a wide range of workplace hazards in manufacturing, warehousing, services, maintenance, healthcare, and other general industry settings. These standards define minimum requirements for physical safeguards, equipment, training, procedures, and documentation.

Part 1910 covers many topics, including walking-working surfaces, emergency action plans, hazardous materials, machine guarding, lockout/tagout, electrical safety, personal protective equipment, fire protection, and more. When a hazard exists in a general industry workplace, there is often a specific 1910 standard that defines exactly how it must be controlled. Compliance with Part 1910 is the baseline expectation — employers who meet OSHA standards are meeting the minimum legal requirement.

When workers recognize a hazard, they should take immediate safe action: stop using unsafe equipment, warn coworkers, report the hazard to a supervisor, and follow established workplace procedures. Reporting is not a disruption — it is how hazards get corrected before someone is seriously hurt.
lessons.employee-rights:
**Employee Rights Under OSHA — OSH Act Section 11(c)**

The OSH Act gives workers important rights that support their ability to participate in workplace safety. Employees have the right to a safe and healthful workplace — one where recognized hazards have been identified and controlled. They have the right to receive information and training about hazards in a language they understand. They have the right to review workplace injury and illness records, and to request an OSHA inspection if they believe hazardous conditions exist.

One of the most important protections under the OSH Act is the prohibition on retaliation. Section 11(c) makes it illegal for employers to discharge, discriminate against, or take adverse action against any employee because they reported a hazard, filed an OSHA complaint, participated in an inspection, or exercised any other right protected by the Act. Employees who experience retaliation have the right to file a complaint with OSHA within 30 days.

These rights only function when workers feel safe using them. A workplace where employees fear consequences for speaking up is a workplace where hazards go unreported and incidents go unaddressed. Supervisors and managers play a critical role in creating an environment where raising a safety concern is seen as a contribution, not a problem.
lessons.employer-responsibilities:
**Employer Responsibilities Under OSHA — General Duty Clause, Section 5(a)(1)**

OSHA's General Duty Clause requires every employer to provide employees with a workplace that is free from recognized hazards that are causing or likely to cause death or serious physical harm. This obligation exists even when no specific OSHA standard covers the hazard in question — employers cannot avoid responsibility simply because a hazard is not explicitly listed in a regulation.

Beyond the General Duty Clause, employers must comply with all applicable OSHA standards, examine workplace conditions to verify they conform to standards, ensure employees have and use required PPE, and provide required training in the hazards and controls relevant to each worker's job. Employers must also maintain required records, post the OSHA poster where workers can see it, report severe injuries (hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye) to OSHA within 24 hours, and report work-related fatalities within 8 hours.

Compliance requires action — not just written policies. Hazard control programs, training schedules, inspection routines, and accountability structures are all part of what it means to meet employer obligations under the OSH Act. Supervisors who overlook known hazards, discourage reporting, or fail to follow up on safety concerns are not meeting the employer's obligation.
lessons.inspections-enforcement:
**OSHA Inspections, Complaints, and Enforcement — 29 CFR Part 1903**

OSHA enforces its standards through workplace inspections conducted by Compliance Safety and Health Officers (CSHOs). Inspections may be triggered by workplace fatalities or catastrophes, formal employee complaints, referrals from other agencies, programmed targeting of high-hazard industries, or follow-up visits to verify that previously cited hazards have been corrected. OSHA prioritizes inspections based on the severity and imminence of the hazard.

When an inspection occurs, the CSHO may conduct opening and closing conferences, review records and written programs, interview employees privately, and walk the facility to identify hazards. Employees have the right to accompany the inspector during the walkthrough and to speak with the inspector confidentially. Employers have the right to require a warrant if OSHA arrives unannounced, though most employers cooperate without one.

If violations are found, OSHA may issue citations requiring employers to correct the hazard within a set timeframe and pay a penalty. Violations are classified by severity — other than serious, serious, willful, repeat, and failure to abate. The goal of enforcement is not punishment alone — it is to ensure that hazardous conditions are corrected so that workers are not harmed. The best outcome is that an inspection finds no violations because the employer is already managing hazards proactively.
lessons.recordkeeping:
**Injury and Illness Recordkeeping — 29 CFR Part 1904**

OSHA's recordkeeping standard, 29 CFR Part 1904, requires most employers with 11 or more employees to maintain a log of work-related injuries and illnesses. The primary forms are the OSHA 300 Log (log of work-related injuries and illnesses), the OSHA 300A (annual summary), and the OSHA 301 (incident report). The 300A must be posted in the workplace from February 1 through April 30 each year.

Not every work-related injury or illness is recordable. An injury or illness must be recorded if it results in days away from work, restricted duty, transfer to another job, medical treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness, or a diagnosis of a significant injury or illness by a healthcare professional. Employers must record these cases within seven calendar days of learning about them.

Accurate recordkeeping is not just a compliance obligation — it is a hazard identification tool. Reviewing injury and illness trends helps employers and safety managers see where hazards are concentrated, what types of incidents are most common, and whether corrective actions are working. Suppressing or failing to record injuries hides the very information needed to improve safety. OSHA prohibits employers from discouraging or retaliating against employees for reporting work-related injuries and illnesses.
lessons.safety-culture:
**Safety Culture and Shared Responsibility — 29 CFR Part 1910**

A safety culture is the shared set of values, beliefs, and behaviors that define how an organization approaches workplace safety. In a strong safety culture, safety is not just a compliance requirement — it is a core value that drives every decision, from how work is designed to how hazards are reported and corrected. Organizations with strong safety cultures consistently experience lower injury rates, fewer near misses that go unreported, and more proactive hazard identification.

Key indicators of a strong safety culture include: employees reporting concerns early without fear of retaliation, supervisors responding promptly and without blame, near misses being treated as learning opportunities rather than embarrassments, training being current and meaningful rather than a checkbox, and accountability flowing both up and down the organization. When these behaviors are present, hazards are addressed before they cause harm.

Every employee contributes to safety culture through their daily choices — whether to report a hazard or ignore it, whether to follow a safety procedure or take a shortcut, whether to speak up or stay silent. OSHA supports safety culture through its Voluntary Protection Programs (VPP) and through recognition of workplaces that go beyond minimum compliance. Building a positive safety culture is ongoing work, not a one-time initiative.
